utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you and good afternoon to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours my name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, as well as our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, my name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones we represent the defence of Mr. Naser Oric. With us today is our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you and your team. So I think the first part of today's hearing we'll be hearing proper, the trial, because we are going to deal with the site visit, I'm going to proceed with the process verbal and therefore this part of the proceedings is not -- does not form part of the pre-Defence conference but of the trial proceedings proper. As I promised you following the site visit that we had in north-eastern Bosnia, and Herzegovina, we are now going to read out a process verbal relating to the visit because we believe that such a process verbal should go into the record, and after that, after reading this, I would like a feedback from you as regards photos which we have and also a video taken during the helicopter flight in case you would like to have it exhibited in the records of the case, which we are ready to do. So this is a process verbal on the site -- on-site visit in Bosnia-Herzegovina which this Trial Chamber conducted between the 20th and the 24th of June 2005. The purpose of the visit was to view some of the sites which are relevant to the case before us. The site visit was planned several months ago in consultation with the parties, the Registrar, and the Chief of Security and his staff of this Tribunal. The parties were advised from the very beginning to agree on a protocol acceptable to both, particularly in view of the fact of the unavoidable absence of the Accused during the on-site visit. During the site visit, the Trial Chamber was accompanied by two members of its staff, as well as by lead counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Jan Wubben, and co-counsel for the Defence, Mr. John Jones. Both parties had an interpreter and an investigator accompanying them. Mr. Philip Berikoff accompanied the Trial Chamber during the entire visit and acted as guide, after that both parties agreed on his choice as guide. Indeed, I want to start by publicly thanking these three gentlemen, without whose corporation the site visit would not have materialised. Their conduct throughout and their cooperation with one another and with the Trial Chamber was exemplary and is to be commended. We also wish to underline Mr. Berikoff's hard work in this whole venture, the rectitude with which he fulfilled his role as a guide, and his great sense of responsibilities towards the well being and safety of all those taking part in the site visit, officials of this Tribunal as well as others. A protocol was agreed to and signed by the parties prior to departure, pursuant to which there were to be no submissions made by either party during the site visit and that the relative explanation of the guide should -- would not include any reference to submissions or to specific facts except in so far as may be agreed upon by the parties. The Trial Chamber is pleased to note that both parties, as well as the guide, Mr. Berikoff, strictly adhered to this protocol during the visit and the Trial Chamber wishes to publicly acknowledge this and express our appreciation to the parties and to the guide. The Trial Chamber also wishes to publicly acknowledge the sterling work done by the security section of this Tribunal, both prior to and in preparation of the site visit, as well as while it was being conducted. The performance of the Tribunal's security team that accompanied us was highly professional and equally very effective. During the visit, the Chamber and the rest of the team were also assisted by EUFOR and in particular we wish to publicly acknowledge the contribution of the Italian carabinieri team who escorted us wherever we travelled and provided us with logistics, cover and protection as well as the Czech contingent that provided of -- EUFOR that provided us with a helicopter and crew which made it possible for us to view from the air most of the area involved in this case, and the terrain which was not practically to reach by car. We also wish to acknowledge the full and effective cooperation of the security and police forces of Republika Srpska and of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Last but not least I wish to thank, publicly thank Mr. Hans Holthuis, Registrar of this Tribunal, who provided not only the funds necessary to make this possible, this site visit, but also the assistance of his staff whenever it was needed. Mr. Holthuis was amongst the very first in this Tribunal to realise the importance of such site visits and the work of the various Trial Chambers and has been instrumental in making them possible. And I publicly acknowledge this. My two colleagues and I have already signed letters of thanks and appreciation to Mr. Innell, Chief of Security of this Tribunal. Major Milan Kutni [phoen] responsible for the Czech contingent with EUFOR, Colonello Giovanni Trulijo [phoen], IPU commander at EUFOR headquarters, the respective commanders of Republika Srpska and the Bosnian federation security and police sections, and several high officials of this Tribunal that I don't need to mention here. Several locations were visited on three consecutive days, that is 21 to 23 of June 2005. The following is a detailed account of the locations visited by the Trial Chamber. I will start with Tuesday, the 21st of June 2005. On Tuesday, 21st of June 2005, the visit started with a stop in Cerska. On the way to Cerska we saw Rovasi. We then drove through Konjevic Polje, where the school was pointed out to us. We drove on to Kravica where we passed the warehouse on the main road. A short stop was made at the elementary school and medical dispensary in the centre of the town. Siljkovici could be seen from Kravica. We then drove on up the hill to Opravdici from Kravica. From a high point, Jezestica could be seen to the right and another small village, possibly Mandici, could the seen to the left I think possibly because there was some doubt forthcoming on whether the village we were being addressed to look at was in actual fact Mandici or not, and I'm still undecided and we are still undecided whether it was Mandici or not. We then drove up above Kravica in the direction of Siljkovici to the power substation -- electrical power substation from where we could see Kravica centre. At the bottom of the hill, there was a monument under construction in memory of the Serb soldiers who fell in the area. The convoy then took the direction of Bozici, which the conditions of the terrain prohibited us from reaching. And so we drove on to Jezestica and the areas of Glogova and Magasici which were pointed out to us. We also visited Bratunac where we first stopped at the purported Vuk Karadzic school but the Defence submitted that this was the wrong school. We therefore were directed to the former Vuk Karadzic school in the centre of the town which the Defence claimed to be the school which is relevant to the case. The health centre in Bratunac was also pointed out to us by the Defence. We also had the opportunity to notice the location of the Drina River on the left when exiting Bratunac in the direction of Voljavica with on the other side of the river. We then proceeded to drive by Voljavica and Zaluzje and proceeded up the hill to the site of a former mosque next to which the Orthodox Sase monastery has now been constructed. We drove down the hill, stopping at the Sase mine, the zinc mine, and the convoy then also drove through Bjelovac from where we could also notice the layout of the Drina River as well as the village of Grabovica across the river and in Serbia. We then were taken on to Loznicka Rijeka and Sikiric, and Vrhpolje. A village across the river and in Serbia could be seen from Sikiric. I now come to Wednesday, 22nd of June. On Wednesday, the 22nd of June, again because of the difficulties we had in reaching some areas, we started with a helicopter flight which lasted an hour and 15 minutes. And which covered the major sites of the visit, even those which we actually then visited by car. The helicopter took off and landed in Vlasenica and flew over Opravdici, Siljkovici, Kravica, Bozici, Glogova, Magasici, Bradjevina, Ratkovici, Ducici, Srebrenica, and Bajramovici. The helicopter flight also gave us a unique opportunity to view the layout of the terrain in various places as well as the flow of the Drina River. Back on the ground, we drove through Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje again. We then passed the area of the Glogova valley and leaving Bratunac behind and continuing along the Drina River on the Bosnian side we saw Grabovica Rijeka. Bradjevina was not visited because of accessibility and road safety concerns that were communicated to us and with which we agreed. The Trial Chamber also stopped at Fakovici where we walked to the school and the post office. We then drove on to Zanjevo and Abdulici, where we stopped briefly. We passed by Radijevici and Divovici, which are two very small hamlets attached to Zanjevo and Abdulici. All four hamlets form a line along the main road facing the Drina River on the Bosnian side. We then headed towards Skelani where we walked halfway across the steel bridge. From Skelani we also had an opportunity to observe Bajna Basta in Serbia on the other side of the Drina. Driving on, we drove into the area of Jezero and Vitez. We then headed towards the village of Osmace on top of a plateau. Next we reached Poznanovici where nothing but the ruins of two buildings remain. The road to Ratkovici and Ducici were -- was impassable and we had to turn back. Coming down through the valley we drove past Kragljivoda and Zeleni Jadar. We reached the Bracan area, drove past the Bracan mine, bauxite mine and elevation, as well as the Gunjaci mine. I come to the last day. We started off on Thursday, the 23rd of June, by going to the village of Suceska. A very small village, and situated on a plateau about ten kilometres from Srebrenica. From there we took the mountain road through Bajramovici to enter Srebrenica from the north end. In Srebrenica, we started by visiting the municipal building and the building behind it which are both to the side of the department store. Attached to the latter, behind the Court building, and separated by a red brick wall, we were able to see the pre-war TO headquarters building. The building behind the municipal building would also be entered by a flight of stairs and the court building part of which the Trial Chamber had the opportunity to see. On the occasion of visiting the building behind the municipal building, the Trial Chamber encountered some unfortunate organisational problems in that the chief judge in Srebrenica, who possessed the only key to allow access to this building was unavailable. We were told he was having breakfast, and the building had to be broken into as he himself sent a message and suggested that we could do. This was the only instance of lack of cooperation that the Trial Chamber encountered during its visit and we thought it fit to mention it in this process verbal, hoping that there will not be a repetition of such incidents in the future. The inside of this building could be seen in part because at ground-floor level the corridor and the rooms are filled with about 10 centimetres of stale water. In Srebrenica, we also saw from outside the Dom Kulture, the culture hall, in the centre of down. We also saw from outside the Domavija hotel. The Trial Chamber also had an opportunity to enter into the old SUP building which is 300 or 400 metres from the centre in the direction of Potocari. We had an opportunity to see the cell with bars, with iron bars, to which some witnesses had referred in the course of the trial. The first floor which was alleged to have housed the civilian police is now a residential floor and we could therefore only see the layout from the landing as no arrangements had been made to have access to the rooms or if they had been made, they had not been implemented. The Prosecution insisted that the judges visit the basement but the door of the only room that there is in the basement was locked and through the key hole it became apparent that it was now being used as a storage area. Part of the landing leading to the basement was blocked with firewood logs. In Srebrenica, we also entered the new PTT building and had a tour of the rooms at first-floor level. From in front of this building, the Srebrenica hospital mentioned during the trial could be seen from outside across the road. This hospital is not being used at present. Exiting Srebrenica from that end we drove on to Potocari which is very close to Srebrenica and situated in a wide valley. We stopped at the Potocari memorial situated just opposite the former DutchBat compound and from the memorial, the different elevations and in particular Kaolin and Caus were pointed out to us by Mr. Jones for the Defence. The last site of the visit was the yellow bridge in Potocari a few metres away. The Trial Chamber returned to The Hague on Friday, the 24th of June. I'm soon going to close this section. I would like to know from both of you if you would like -- we have a set of photos that we have taken ourselves and we also have the video of the helicopter flight which the Italian crew took and made available. Do you want those to enter into the records or not? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't had the opportunity yet to review the videos, as you may know we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to take it under consideration, if you don't mind, particularly as we -- I think there may also be a couple of videos. You'll recall, firstly, the process verbal as far as we are concerned is a fair reflection of the visit. Our position was that we hadn't seen from the air, we the Defence team -- a video was made I think by the carabinieri, and I haven't had the opportunity to review that video yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if it's been proposed that would be an exhibit. In any event, if I could revert to you on -- on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my suggestion to you is the following: I have taken note of what Mr. Wubben has said. With regard to photos, what's your position? You want to see them too or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are these the photographs taken by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By Mr. Tujman [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. They -- despite the fact that some of them might not be entirely flattering I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, there are many of them that are not entirely flattering, speaking for myself to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't mind leaving for posterity images of my pockmarked face and complexion. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that case, no objection either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I wouldn't stay we stay selecting photos from -- we just introduce them as they are. With regard to the DVD, I haven't seen it either and the reason is it is DVD and I don't have a DVD in my office, although I have at home. But I've been busy, Mr. Jones, so I haven't had time to stay looking for an hour and a half of DVD. I will see it. I will make sure that you are copied, you will have a copy of this DVD, if you don't have it already, and of course you are free to let us know if you agree to have it tendered in that case it will be our own exhibit or not, and we will do that at our leisure and pleasure. It's not something that needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We have a copy of it. May I also just endorse Your Honour's remarks and the appreciation of the guide and the security section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I also wish to endorse your remarks about the professionalism of Mr. Berikoff and his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I appreciate that, Mr. Jones, because sometimes we don't realise how much work and how much stress it involves for them, and God forbid something goes wrong, because if something goes wrong then there will be a lot of problems. So I can imagine their stress and I appreciate the professionality that they showed. Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, also I share that appreciation and that's for the record, and in addition to the comment by my learned friend that the process verbal reflects accurately the facts, the locations showed, I can confirm that. But in addition, I would like to share there is only one doubt of a certain location and that reached me afterwards. That's the Kravica warehouse at the main road, as pointed out to us, and I'm not sure any longer whether or not that is the only warehouse and that might be the warehouse that is relevant. I would like to take a contact with the Defence in that respect and to make a submission next week or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Yes, fair enough. So basically that brings to an end the part of today's sitting which is trial proceedings proper. We will continue on Monday, the 4th of July. And we now move to the Pre-Defence Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you are all aware that some time back we signed a scheduling order in preparation of the Pre-Defence Conference, specifying time limits within which we expected the Defence team to proceed with the filings according to Rule 73 -- according to Rule 73 and other applicable Rules of this Tribunal, and in particular to put in the position this Trial Chamber to know what areas would be addressed by the Defence, by which witnesses, and for how long. We had split this into two parts. There was to be a first filing, which was done before the site visit, and a second one which followed after the site visit. They had to be filed in time and were actually filed in time, to enable the Trial Chamber to go through the documents and give directions to our Senior Legal Officer in preparation and for the purposes of the Rule 65 ter meeting that we had scheduled already to take place on the 30th of June. That is yesterday. For the purpose of the 65 ter meeting, we gave specific instructions and directions to our Senior Legal Officer which he was to communicate to the Defence team in particular but also to the parties, leaving him of course with enough flexibility to deal with whatever arose during the 65 ter meeting and without, however, having the authority to bind in any way this Trial Chamber, because it was obvious from the very beginning that there would be Pre-Defence Conference following immediately after the 65 ter meeting. We did, however, ask the Senior Legal Officer to communicate to the Defence that there were several areas which were all included in one way or another in the objects that the Defence team were seeking to adduce evidence about, that we were satisfied, had already been sufficiently proven and we were satisfied that we had already received enough evidence to the extent that we felt we did not require any further evidence on them from the Defence. We also asked our SLO to communicate to the Defence that it was our intention to establish a maximum number of witnesses that they would be allowed, which would not correspond to the total amount of witnesses that they were seeking to adduce and that there would be also a time limit within which the Defence would be called upon, in terms and pursuant to our rules, to finish its case from the evidentiary aspect. The meeting 65 ter meeting was held yesterday. It was a four-hour meeting, I am told, more or less, following which we were given a report by the Senior Legal Officer, detailing the various topics that were discussed and also detailing the position that was taken by the Defence. That doesn't seem to have -- at least not in the report that we have, any position taken by the Prosecution and we stand to be corrected on this as we go along. So I will start first, not because I throw any doubt on what Mr. Von Hebel reported to us, but I want to make sure that his report indeed reflects what was said yesterday and what was discussed yesterday, and then we proceed with the rest of today's agenda. The report that we have received reads as follows: "The Defence submitted the following at the Rule 65 ter conference in response to being informed of the areas the Trial Chamber feels it doesn't need any further evidence about during the Defence case. The areas in which the Trial Chamber -- also the areas in which the Trial Chamber would be interested in hearing witnesses giving evidence, the proposed timetable for completion of the case, and the proposed planning for the Defence case, in terms of number of witnesses and hours which will be permitted. The Senior Legal Officer reports to us the following with regard to the following points. First item or first matter is Defence assessment of time. According to the Defence, the number of Defence witnesses already that is - for the information of everyone, we are talking of 73 witnesses in a case where the witnesses for the Prosecution were roughly 50 - and the number of Defence witnesses, according to the Defence team, already reflects careful consideration of the Rule 98 bis ruling in that the number of witnesses has been trimmed down to 73 from 200. The Defence also contends that its case should take 120 trial days to complete, including time for the Prosecution cross-examination of Defence witnesses. Then I'm informed that the Defence raised some considerations and issues relating to what was termed as completion strategy pressure. The Senior Legal Officer was told by the Defence that Security Council Resolution 1581 indicating a completion date for this case along with a letter from the president to the Security Council concerning the same matter make it appear that completion strategy pressure is affecting limitations placed on the length of the Defence team -- case. The second point made by the Defence according to our Senior Legal Officer in this context is that if the completion strategy is a concern, the Prosecution should have limited -- should have been limited to four or five months. The next issue that was taken up by the Defence during yesterday's meeting deals with equality of arms. According to the Defence team, equality of arms meanings that the Defence should be permitted to have and bring forward the same number of witnesses and time as the Prosecution. The question was asked, "If equality of arms doesn't mean resources or time, what does it mean?" It was also submitted that it is not possible to compare this case to other cases since each Defence strategy is different. The aspect of the complexity of the case was also dealt with and the following points made by the Defence team according to our SLO: 13 separate criminal actions are charged with regard to the attacks on the villages, plus the detention charges, for example individual villages are alleged to have been attacked by multiple units under Oric's command so a witness is needed from each unit per attacked village. Second point is command responsibility is alleged to include failure to punish up to 1995 and the Celebici judgement lists eight factors Defence must consider in this regard. Next point, always in this context, is the Defence need to challenge every portion, even minor, of the Prosecution case, to include attacking credibility of witnesses and challenging authenticity of documents. Last, elimination of the plunder charges has no effect on the number of witnesses to be called, since same witnesses are required for wanton destruction. With regard to the various indications of matters that the Trial Chamber would not require evidence upon, as communicated to the Defence team by the SLO yesterday, the Defence, we are told, had the following submissions: The areas in which the Trial Chamber says it is satisfied are not agreed facts. The Defence needs the Trial Chamber to give legal effect by an order with findings. The Appeals Chamber might not be satisfied that these areas have been established and the Defence must consider this possibility. Finally, the Defence doesn't want to rely on these areas and later have them used against it. Then we come to the background of Srebrenica. According to the Defence, they must be allowed to present evidence on Srebrenica and ethnic cleansing. According to the Defence, nothing in the record so far exists which accepts that the Serb attacks came from Serbian villages around Srebrenica which were later the object of attack. And then there is an affirmation by the Defence that they are not trying a political case or intending to offer evidence about the war in general. It is obvious that the meeting yesterday came to a stalemate. There was no apparent way to come to an agreement, and I am told by the Senior Legal Officer that there was a reaction from the Defence team which consisted of the following. Of course, they would consider lodging an appeal, but they were not certain as to which court. They pointed out that I, as Presiding Judge, may find myself in conflict if only I can request extension of ad litem judges rather than those judges themselves, and also, they expressed doubts about the president of this Tribunal alleging that he would have a conflict of interest due to his letter to the Security Council. So the Defence team said that they would also contemplate not calling any witnesses at all, and as a last resort, I'm told, they also suggested that they could withdraw -- consider withdrawing as counsel from the case. This is the report that we have from Mr. Von Hebel. My first question, and I want a straight yes or no answer, for the time being, is whether you agree, both of you, that this is a truthful reflection of what was discussed and what was said yesterday. I think it concerns you more than Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it has to be a yes or no I would have to say no. I would prefer to just briefly clarify where I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will move to that straight away because it's important that we move today. And while we move to that, I would also like to hear from you whether you stick to the same position that you took yesterday or whether there are any other suggestions or other positions that you might consider taking. That will be followed -- that will be followed by a detailed explanation on our part of how we see the entire scenario relating to the administration proper, administration of the Defence team pursuant to what we are requested to do by Rule 73 ter and then we will also have another opportunity to address the Trial Chamber on our suggestions and then ultimately we will come down with a written decision which will be handed down probably on Monday. It will be a written decision. Mr. Wubben, do you consider the report that I have just read as more or less truthful -- not truthful, faithful rendition of the proceedings of the 65 ter meeting held yesterday under the auspices of Mr. -- or the chairmanship of Mr. Von Hebel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is a summary but it is a true reflection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a summary. Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour firstly I should just say that we actually have a transcript now, and of course there is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, let's take the matter of the transcript. It was my intention, having discussed that with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, that the transcript should -- this is the first time in the history of this Tribunal that a 65 ter meeting, a preparation of a Defence team -- a Defence case, has ended up the way it has ended, and it's the first time in the history of this Tribunal that a Defence team, with the exception of Milosevic, has tried to adduce more evidence than the Prosecution and has tried to adduce more documents practically than the Prosecution itself. So I think it's the case of putting in the record the transcript of yesterday's 65 ter meeting because I want to have everything clear for whatever purposes it might be needed later on. The only problem that I have is the following: I am told -- I am not -- I was not aware of then that usually that transcript would be a confidential one. I do not contest it. What I would like to know from you, whether you want to keep it treated as confidential, in which case it would go under seal, or whether you would like to have it publicly filed at our instance which we would prefer but we will not force it on you, of course, in which case it would be filed publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would be delighted for it to be public. We would have asked for it ourself because we did expound at great length all our reasons for being -- I'll come to it, both for being greatly shocked by the suggestion that we should having 25 per cent of the time allocated to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so we would be very happy for it to be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed it is the first time so I would like to ask some time to enable Prosecutor to take responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Not later than Monday, please. Monday we will decide whether it goes private or under seal. For the time being, I think it can go in, and it will remain under seal until Monday when we can unseal it. That's the position. Yes, now, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, firstly, I think, particularly since we are not sure yet whether the 65 ter Conference will be public or not, we need today to be able to expound our grave, grave concerns that our client's prospects for a fair trial are rapidly vanishing over the horizon with the present directions for the Defence case. So I would ask that today my colleague and I both be given half an hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- To do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you deserve half an hour, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your colleague I -- Oh, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Lead counsel, half an hour; myself, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I want to be moderate in my remarks but you will have seen our reaction yesterday and I also don't want to mince my words. I do want it to be absolutely clear on the record that we feel that if we are only allowed 25 per cent of the Prosecution -- the time the Prosecution took that it would -- it would be a sham. It would be a mockery of justice, to make it absolutely clear. And we do maintain our position that the completion strategy is being given precedence over a fair trial. I'm not going to go into those -- my remarks now, the body of remarks. I will come to those presently. It was really just to deal with the summary by Mr. Von Hebel which I was forced to give a yes or no answer as to whether it was accurate. It's mostly accurate but there are some clarifications which I want to make so that our position isn't made to sound ridiculous because in some respects, our position is being -- firstly, by being compared to the case of Milosevic is being made to look as if we are being unreasonable. I'd like to deal actually with Milosevic just while we are on that subject, that it's not just Slobodan Milosevic who wanted as much time or more time, but the Trial Chamber said in its order dated the 25th of February 2004, "Considering that the accused should have the same time as the Prosecution had to present his, the accused's case in chief." In that case a proper -- a Trial Chamber properly considered that the equality of arms meant that the Defence should have the same time to present his case as the Prosecution had to present theirs. And, you know, I ask the question, is there one rule for Slobodan Milosevic and another rule for Naser Oric? Surely not. In terms of the summary, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one rule, it's equality of arms, which I can tell you straight and plain from the very beginning, cannot be measured by the number of witnesses, by the same number of witnesses or by the same time or by the same number of hours. It is not qualified by numbers, Mr. Jones, nowhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But surely it's not one week for us and eight months for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one spoke of one week, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of these -- the points made by -- in the report, firstly we didn't say that we had a list of 200 witnesses. It's that we interviewed more than 200 witnesses and that we've trimmed the number down, a small qualification but an important one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, no, that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We didn't maintain that we have to call one witness for each unit involved in each action. We pointed out that, for example in Bijelovac, if there are 15 units which are alleged to be under the command of Naser Oric, that of course, we have a right to bring evidence concerning whether that unit was actually present, whether they were under Oric's command or something else. And the idea that two witnesses which we were told we could have for each action, the idea that they could cover what 15 units were doing in an area of several kilometres square is not adequate. So we weren't saying we need one witness per unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because I am sure that this will be reflected later on in your submissions. The way it was put to you yesterday may have led you to understand that we were limiting you by numbers to each and every incident et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, two witnesses per action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what we meant. What we meant was that in our considerations having gone through your document, we were under the firm conviction that that particular area of the indictment could be covered by two or three witnesses. That is our own exercise. You are not going to be limited by a number to each and every incident that arises out of the indictment but you are going to be limited by the number of witnesses that you will be allowed to bring forward. And how you distribute that, how you present your Defence, is none of the concern of this Tribunal but before we could come to the conclusion as to how many witnesses to allow you to bring forward, considering also that we are enlisting a large number of facts and issues which we feel there is absolutely no need for the Defence to bring forward evidence about, that would give you more than ample opportunity to defend your client as -- in the best possible manner. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Avoid -- I know it was put to you the way it was put and the way it is reflected, but it is not the intention of the Trial Chamber to tell you with regard to the attack on Jezestica, two witnesses, that's up to you. But we are going to tell you, as regards the entire indictment, you are going to have this much and not more. And not only we have to do that but it is put on us as an obligation by our Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm aware of that. I'm grateful for that clarification. There's -- all of these matters are matters which my colleague will address and I myself will address at a certain moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I wanted to make this -- this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I almost feel obliged pre-emptively to make now, which is just to dispel any of -- of unreasonableness on our -- our part, just to observe that in the Kordic case, the Defence had 62 per cent of the time allocated to the Prosecution; Galic 75 per cent; Stakic 83 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Jones, is it true that yesterday you told Mr. Von Hebel that it is not possible to compare this case to other cases, since each Defence strategy is different?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's not make comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour made the point that this was the first in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is the first case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- to why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not compare --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Already made of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a comparison. That's a statement of fact. Let's not make comparisons; we are not interested in comparisons. You will not be given so many witnesses and not more or -- and so much time and not less or more because that was the case in the other cases. You will be given a maximum number of witnesses which you can bring forward and a maximum time within which to conclude your case because we have studied what you have submitted, we have studied the rest of the case, and we are sure that we can have you complete your exercise of defending your client within the limits that we will be imposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and Your Honour appreciates that we are convinced that with current indications we cannot present our case fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you. You have every right to appeal our decision when it comes down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we will need a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you will need a decision and you will have it on writing. But, of course, on Monday we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may not call any evidence at that point if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Appealing the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we are appealing the decision, Your Honour, we need to have time to appeal your decision and then have the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will do what we say. You -- we will fix Monday for the first day of hearing witnesses and if you don't bring witnesses, you will -- you will need to consider what the consequences will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are appealing we have a right to appeal your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You can't order us to bring witnesses when there is an appeal pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is nothing, Mr. Jones, that would stop us proceeding with the case according to our decisions and in the meantime the Appeals Chamber will have an opportunity to decide. If they decide in your favour, we will prolong the case for the Defence. If they decide in favour of our decision, then obviously, if you haven't adduced evidence in the meantime, you have a big problem on your plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or Your Honours have that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, frankly, it doesn't work that way because if we only have a certain amount of time to bring witnesses we need to know that before we start because if we call four witnesses in the next two weeks and then we are told that in fact the Appeals Chamber upholds your decision that we have a very small period of time to call witnesses, maybe we wouldn't have called those four witnesses but called other ones. So of course it prejudices us deeply to have to call witnesses when we have an appeal ending saying that we should have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your point. Do it whichever way. We are -- I'm telling you it's -- the way you conduct your Defence is your problem, Mr. Jones, and that of Madam Vidovic. It's none of our concern. We will give you a time limit. We will give you a number of -- maximum number of witnesses that you can call. The rest is in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday we start. You make your own calculations and your own guesses but if your calculations go wrong, if your calculations go wrong, then it's your client who is going to suffer. Think twice before you jump to conclusions as to what you're going to do on Monday after that we have handed down our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but please think twice before riding roughshod over the right to a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are not running roughshod. I take objections to your assertions, allegations, just as much as I take objection to the allegation that we are putting the completing -- completion strategy above our considerations of securing to your trial -- to your client a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour said as much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is extremely undignified. It is extremely undignified even to hear that being said in open court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, you said as much in a meeting with the parties that we had to consider, and you pointed to your colleagues, you said you must consider the Security Council may not extend the -- may not extend the times of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You put that to us as a reason why the trial might be shortened. So it is -- Your Honour has told us it's a factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you suggest, Mr. Jones, that if I come to the conclusion that if it is not possible to conclude this trial within the time limit set by the Security Council, I will feel in conflict with myself, and I will not recommend the extension of the term of office of the two ad litem judges. And if you -- if that's what you think of me and of this Trial Chamber, you are completely mistaken, Mr. Jones, and I never expected this from you. And I will not say anything more except that it is also very undignified on your part and it doesn't do you any good to throw shadows and cast doubts on the integrity of the President of this Tribunal who would, like me, according to you, sacrifice your client's right to a fair trial simply because he has written a letter to the Security Council recommending the extension of the two ad litem judges till a certain time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, I'm not casting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To suggest -- to suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- doubt on his integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's absurd, Your Honour. What I'm hearing is you're saying that he has already taken a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you have said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and therefore I would apply for his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it is impossible to translate this. Please slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you said that you will be mincing your words. To say, to tell the Tribunal that what we are saying is absurd is undignified on your part, and we will not accept such language to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's -- yes, of course, we expect you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The other -- the other point is that Your Honour has said that -- said that -- Your Honour has indicating you're heard enough on certain matters means that we can therefore not bring evidence on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can explain. I will explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, may I make one point in that regard. In my system, certainly, if a judge says you needn't bother me with that, that means you've won on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It means you don't need to bring evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in the 98 bis judgement all we have is a finding that there was a siege, not particularly that it was imposed from the towns and villages in the indictment and that therefore we didn't -- don't need to bring evidence concerning starvation, et cetera. Now, what we need in order to actually be able to rely on findings by the Chamber, that we don't need to bring evidence, is a finding saying we find there was artillery in Siljkovici. We find that the Serbs in Kravica expelled their neighbours and had a strong military presence there and therefore the Defence needn't both to bring evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. What the points that we will be confirming again in open court today, when we spell them out to you and then you will have them in writing, means, yes. It doesn't mean that we don't want you to bring evidence. It means that we have heard enough evidence, the evidence comes from the Prosecution case, and that includes also questions -- answers upon questions upon cross-examination, and we feel that these areas have been completely dealt with and they all go in favour of your client and not against. So you have our commitment that on those issues, nothing remains open. Those issues are clear in our minds. We will have a commitment with the Accused when we come to final judgement, that not a single one of these issues will be put in doubt. In other words, that will be a confirming them as facts that have been sufficiently proved to our satisfaction at the end of the Prosecution case. It goes beyond what was said in Rule 98 bis because for the purpose of the Rule 98 bis it's not only a declaration as to what facts emerge, result, to the satisfaction of the Tribunal. But for the purpose of Rule 98 bis we were dealing with six counts, with the elements relating to each of the six counts. So when we say that there is sufficient evidence on the basis of which we can go -- we can proceed with count 1, or count 3 or count 5, it means basically we can -- but now we are telling you after that we have decided the Rule 98 bis that there are various areas that we needn't hear any further evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but you see -- yes, but we need, of course, to hear from the -- or to see the order of the Chamber so we actually know what precisely the finding is. Because to say we've heard enough evidence, is that because it's considered irrelevant or because the finding is X or Y? Just with agreed facts, we need to know precisely what the Trial Chamber has found so we can work out whether we still need to add to it somewhat or whether -- I appreciate -- the principle is clear and acceptable that once something has been found judicially we don't need to litigate it any further. But current indications were not sufficient to allow us to proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I also understand and grant you unconditionally that in this respect you are 100 per cent right. In other words, when we tell you, for example, we don't need to hear further evidence on the fact that Srebrenica was under siege from, I don't know when until I don't know when, continuously, and that it was being continuously bombarded by artillery and from the air, we are committing ourselves with your client that that is our finding. If, however, there is any area arising out of this finding of the Trial Chamber that doesn't satisfy you or which you think might still leave you exposed later on, then it is your duty to indicate it to us, and if we feel that we don't need evidence even on that, we will tell you. If it's the case of allowing you to bring evidence on that particular point, we will open all doors for you. For example -- I mean, I'm sorry I'm interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. It's a useful clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we come from a jurisdiction where we are used to tackle one another in this fashion. For example, you have the first two witnesses, not -- sorry, not the first two witnesses, the seconds and the third witnesses for this coming week; I don't know the names. Anyway, but it's not the lady who will be coming forward to confirm, not Edina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We weren't sure which witness 3 was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Belgian doctor and the other one who was a member of the SDA and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, so you're referring to the Belgian doctor and Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know the name. I mean don't -- I'm hopeless at names. We are going to tell you we don't need to hear evidence on several issues but many of these issues are already included in what these two witnesses are going to testify, and we are going to allow those two. We are going to allow those two so that we will have a clearer idea whether there are areas where we are sort of closing doors where we would need to open them. If we would need to open them, we will open them, but if we don't need to open them we are not going to let the resources of this Tribunal be spent. You are being paid money that is being paid by other countries, including your own. I and my colleagues are being paid money by other countries, and every single person in this courtroom, with the exception of interns who pay their own way, is being paid by the international community. So please do understand that if I am being hard, if my colleagues with me are being hard, if we are imposing a time limit, if we are imposing a limited number of witnesses that you can bring over, it's not because we wouldn't like or love to tell you, let's take the case until you are completely satisfied that you have brought forward the last of the witnesses that you would feel comfortable to bring forward. It's because we have a responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if the same point can be proved by two witnesses, we have a responsibility to tell you, please, Mr. Jones, refrain from bringing the third and the fourth and the fifth and the sixth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour, but then we do wonder why the Prosecution's case went on for eight months with witnesses giving evidence for days and days where we are being allocated according to our calculations about 2.5 or three hours per witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have experienced enough, Mr. Jones, to realise that what was going on was going to make your case much more simple. And the fact that -- you should be the first one to realise that the Prosecution case has ultimately made your case much more simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed I appreciate that. But there is a related point which I was going to address which was this: That the reason also why we need findings by the Chamber is because it has an application for the credibility of Prosecution witnesses, and that's one of the reasons why we want to address these issues. Because if you have a Prosecution witness who says "I was in the village minding my own business. There were no -- there was no military, no soldiers, no artillery," and we want to prove that there was to show -- to impeach their credibility. If Your Honours say we have enough evidence to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have enough evidence -- we are not going to tell you that we have enough evidence on this ----

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then their credibility remains unimpeached when we have a right to impeach it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. You are going to be allowed to bring your witnesses with regard to the credibility of witnesses that the Prosecution have brought forward. We are never going to tell you, listen, we don't need to receive evidence on what happened in Fakovici during the alleged attack of the - I don't know which date - or Jezestica what happened on the -- during the attack on Jezestica on such and such a date. We are not going to make assumptions there and we are not going to make any findings there. We will make findings after we have concluded your case and we come to the final deliberations. What we are going to tell you we needn't hear any more about are factual matters that we believe have been more than sufficiently covered already by previous witnesses, both as a result of the examination-in-chief, so I want to make myself clear, and also as a result of the questions that the Defence put in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think just after we revisit that issue, if I may just finish clarifying the notes of the summary of the meeting. It's also not the case that we said that we have a right to attack every single point that the Prosecution ever made. It was really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- a slightly more nuanced point than that. It's a point that something which may seem small may be a link in a chain, and so we want to knock out that link rather than just leaving it there, and even if it seems small. And secondly, and this goes back to the last point, if a Prosecution witness completely implausibly states that there was no military presence in his village in, let's say, April 1992, long before the actions, and we can prove that there absolutely was, then of course we have to be able to prove that to show that witness is not credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm referring to us addressing issues which may not go directly to the core of the case for example whether there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which point are you referring to, because I don't recall having mentioned that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was the fifth point of the summary of Mr. Von Hebel that we were insisting on our right to attack every matter mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Every portion, even minor, to attack whether -- and challenging --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may collaterally attack something to show that a witness is not credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's way -- of course, we are not going to stop you when it comes to the credibility of witnesses, Mr. Jones. It would be absolutely crazy to tell you we believed this witness and we believe the other witness and we believe these witnesses and you are not going to bring evidence to prove the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why we are saying we need more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but we have made our calculations, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The sixth point was that I didn't say that there was no affect on the plunder charges being dropped. But it was that there was not a great difference made by that, because all the actions remain and so we would have had witnesses covering wanton destruction and plunder again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm also glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, I think there were just a couple of points. I think the seventh point was that -- was to do with the siege that -- Your Honour is accepting that there was a siege, again perhaps I made this point, but we are not content with finding that there was a siege without it being clear that the very villages in the indictment were the siege. It's being -- it's the fact of being surrounded by hostile villagers and hostile villages or village guards or Italians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is going to be granted to you, Mr. Jones, so you don't need to worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The places in the indictment. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, just on appeal, I do want to make absolutely clear that when I say we would have to apply or possibly might apply to disqualify a judge, it's the appearance of justice and the fact that if a judge seems to have taken a position in the litigation due to a prior association that we could consider applying for them not to sit on the appeal ... But that's not -- it's not an attacking their integrity. It's a very common place occurrence, one can think of Lord Hoffman in the House of Lords in the Pinochet case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the way it was put to us, Mr. Jones. You know that the composition of the Trial Chamber almost exceptionally includes the President himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a question of writing about the length of the trial before we had made our opinions clear on how long we thought our trial would be and that might reflect a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The President acts on my advice. The President acts on my advice, which changes from time to time according to the circumstances. If you were to convince me today that you need another year to conclude your case I may grant you another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may yet consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if I am convinced that you need one week, I will not grant you more than one week. When I say "I," it doesn't mean I. I mean, I have a habit of saying "I." I don't mean to -- I can assure you that in all these matters we are in constant consultation, Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt, and we all agree on one part, on one thing, and that is you will get all the time that you require. But we decide the time that you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have to decide if that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I mean, of course. I mean that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally that just brings me possibly to the last point which is that certainly while we stated that we may present no evidence because if I may present a metaphor which occurred to me in this context, litigation is often compared to a tennis match, and we -- and this -- this is currently the second week of Wimbledon, that if one had a match in which the Prosecution is presented with a brand new racket and we were presented with a racket with a few strings that have been snipped and half a shaft, and told, "Go ahead and play," who would play under those circumstances? Those watching the Trial or the match are not going to see that we've got half a racket; they are just going to see us losing. And another analogy, it's as if one had a budget of a 100 dollars for rackets and 80 dollars goes to the Prosecution, 20 dollars to us - that's the eight months and two months - who would play under those circumstances? And so when we say that we may not call evidence, we mean that we -- it's not in our view better to have ten witnesses or 20 witnesses or no witnesses. It may be better to bring no evidence whatsoever. But certainly, it's no not a position that we would withdraw. We're not going to leave our client high and dry under any circumstances. So I want that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sure of. That -- even if I were told -- I was told yesterday that at the end during an apocalyptic sort of fit, you said you might even consider withdrawing completely from the case. I know who I am dealing with. So I know your great sense of responsibility, Mr. Jones, and that's because I'm addressing you, but I also know the great sense of responsibility of Madam Vidovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I want to make it clear that I also know that in your heart of hearts, you know what the consequences would be if you decide not to bring forward evidence. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It depends on how strong the Prosecution's case is at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but if -- it depends on how strong the Prosecution case is. But then, if you feel that the Prosecution case is not strong, you don't come forward with 73 witnesses. And if you feel that the Prosecution case is strong, you don't think of providing or offering as a solution the -- not bringing any witnesses at all. So I am sure that we can talk sense and that we will approach this and finalise and come to a conclusion in a rational manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm also sure that you will of course have ample opportunity to go to the appeal if our decision will not be to your liking. But we are also making it clear that we have a responsibility to go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say one thing before we move on to the next stage of this, which is just that we are not calling 73 witnesses because we think the Prosecution case is strong. My 98 bis submission was this whole case should have been thrown out and I stand behind that 1.000 per cent. We are calling 73 witnesses because we think the account which was presented by Prosecution witnesses is so false in its entirety, and this is Srebrenica and the 10th anniversary of the genocide of which is coming up, that this Tribunal has a truth-finding role which Your Honour has repeatedly emphasised. And to do justice to that, we need to correct that picture. But this is certainly not because we think the Prosecution evidence is strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what is worrying me, Mr. Jones, because reading through the lines of Mr. Von Hebel's report, and also listening to what he had to tell me upon questions that I put to him, I got the impression that you think that it is possible for you to turn this trial towards particular direction, which I am telling you straight and plain we are not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've repeated -- we've said I don't know on how many occasions, we're not -- we have no political agenda. We're not trying to show anything about 95. My point is this, and it's perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour? Perhaps it's met by the suggestion that Your Honours will actually make findings. But as things currently stand and as things currently stand we are proposing 73 witnesses because we say there is this complete false account from 92, 93, and what was happening in Srebrenica, the whole context of which is absolutely relevant for Article 73. I'm sorry, this isn't a case of "Did our client pull a trigger or not," it's a case of whether he had control over thousands of people. And the context I'm sorry, is relevant to that, and in the context as presented by Prosecution, we say, is completely false. That's why we want 73 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to that. We will tell you what you don't need to stick to. And what we will tell you should in your mind rectify what you describe as a perverted description of the events and the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we said it from the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we wanted to make clear from the outset, and we want to send the message loud and clear, that in this trial we are not trying the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We know no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not trying the Serbian people. We are not going to issue a certificate of good conduct and of heroism and heroic acts to the authorities in Srebrenica or authorities in Bosnia that lived and fought the siege of Srebrenica. We are not going to hand out any medals. What we have is one single person here, Mr. Oric, that is being charged, stands charged with just four counts now, two relating to inhumane treatment, cruel treatment, and murder which the Prosecution is not alleging that he has committed himself but that he is responsible for under 7(3), and that's the whole thing. I mean whether these people existed, whether these people were inhumanely treated or killed, whether in any case -- in any manner whatsoever, under the law governing 7(3) responsibility, your client could be found guilty or not. We are not dealing now whether your client was the commander of thousands and thousands of troops. We are dealing on whether he had effective control and those two places, over those guards, whether it was possible for him to prevent what happened, if it indeed happened, and if, irrespective of there, whether actually there was a failure on his part to punish, if he was in a position to punish. And that's what we are interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't forget, Mr. Jones, and I'm sure you don't need to be reminded about this, that you don't carry any burden of proof. There is no small item in this case, no issue, which has emerged in such a way that has shifted the burden of proof from the Prosecution on to you, on to the Defence. The same applies to the wanton destruction. If we are talking of military necessity, it's the Prosecution that has to prove military necessity. If the Prosecution has asserted that in the attack on Bjelovac, the following 10, 15 units took part and has not brought one single witness to confirm who was taking part in those units, are you going to bring the evidence yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We were invited to fill in some gaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But are you going to bring the evidence yourself? You don't carry a burden of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We are aware of all these principles, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last thing I would want to hear from you is thank you for letting me know this. This is the first time I come to learn about these. I know you know about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if I may also call my colleague, we are getting into the substance of these issues now and there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it will reduce the discussion later in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but I wonder if my lead counsel could address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I was going -- before Madam Vidovic addresses us, we have how many minutes, ten minutes? We can take ten minutes and I will update you on the areas where we are going to tell you that we do not require any evidence from you. So that then you will have the break, you will discuss it amongst you, and you can react afterwards, after having -- having, having heard what we have to say. All right? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these are the areas that we will not require evidence from you. Now, I must make a small caveat. I also said that with regard to certain of these -- some of these matters that I will be mentioning, in actual fact, at the same time we are telling you we don't require evidence. But at the same time we are going to allow you the first two witnesses that are coming next week. I mean, you know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There will be issues of bringing, if it comes to that, bringing different witnesses in the second week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it Izet Redzic and Eric Dachy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So when we read the summary of Izet Redzic, indeed he is going to cover several of the points that we are going to tell you we don't need further evidence from you. In telling you we don't need further evidence from you, we have also taken into consideration the fact that we anticipate this gentleman to testify on those things. The same applies to Eric Dachy, who will be testifying on certain matters that we will be telling you we don't need any further evidence from you. But we are going to tell you we don't need further evidence upon you because already we are satisfied that we don't need further evidence. But we are also satisfied that with the evidence of Dr. Eric Dachy, we will be further satisfied that we don't need any further evidence from you. Did we make ourselves clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. These are the points. Please make a note of them. I will go through them slowly. Number 1. There is a variation on some of the matters from the way it was communicated to you by Mr. Von Hebel. It's not because Mr. Von Hebel communicated something to you which he was not authorised to communicate, but because we have had discussions, further discussions, and we have had second thoughts about certain issues. We have added a couple of other matters. So let's start from here. The historical and political backgrounds which led to the war in April of 1992. This, we believe we have heard enough. Part of this will also be covered by the witness Izet Redzic and we do not expect you to bring forward any evidence on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still confused. Will there be findings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm telling you these are going to be findings. These are going to be incorporated in a written decision. It basically means a commitment of this Trial Chamber with Mr. Oric that he will not have to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When I mean a finding [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When I refer to finding, I mean not just saying that we don't need to hear about it, but saying that we find that the war started when ethnic cleansing occurred in eastern Bosnia, Serb forces and paramilitary, et cetera. A finding to that effect which we could use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A finding. For example, you asked about ethnic cleansing. We are going to tell you we don't need any further evidence about ethnic cleansing because we are telling you that we have sufficient evidence in the records of the case, arising from the same evidence of the Prosecution, which shows that there was ethnic cleansing by the Serbs on a large scale in the area relevant to this indictment. Do you want me to say more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would be grateful to know what the findings are, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, well that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to tell you there was ethnic cleansing in the village of Vlasenica on such and such a date. We are going to tell you there was ethnic cleansing throughout -- before the period relevant to this indictment, during the period relevant to this indictment, and after the period relevant to this indictment because this emerges from the same evidence of the Prosecution. So you don't need to address any -- adduce any evidence to tell us there was ethnic cleansing. We are granting you that there was ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just wish that the findings, those findings being read now so we can actually know what we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am going to read them one after the other. There is why I think perhaps we may have been more clear yesterday, but I think we were also not understood completely. So -- so the first is the historical and political background which led to the war in April 1992. In actual fact we are not attaching too much importance to this fact. We find very little relevance for the purpose of this case. But we do have enough in evidence already. The second point is - I go slowly, Mr. Jones - the large number of attacks by Serbs, and when I say Serbs, I mean also Serb forces, all right? By Serbs on villages in the area, including the wanton destruction and plunder of Muslim villages and the laying of mines by Serb forces in and around destroyed Muslim villages and hamlets. This you don't need to address because we are granting it as already sufficiently proved for the purposes of our exercise. The killing and inhumane treatment of Muslims, and that is civilians and non-civilians alike, by Serbs or Serb forces, for whatever it is worth. The policy of ethnic cleansing by the Serbs, and Serbs I mean be it the SDS, the political authorities, and the forces, before, during, and after events in and around Srebrenica, in and around Srebrenica. Next point is general evidence or evidence of a generic nature - that's better English - of positive treatment of Serbs, be they civilians or not, hostages or wounded, in Muslim hospitals, including the one in Srebrenica by Muslims. We don't need to hear evidence on that. But if the evidence that you would like to adduce relates to the persons that are mentioned in counts 1 and 2, then, yes, bring them forward. But if it's in relation to, I don't know which other Serbs, who could be few or could be many, we are not interested to hear more. We have had witnesses from the Prosecution and victims, alleged victims themselves testifying that this was the case. So if you are capable of adducing witnesses testifying about persons that we are interested in, yes. About other persons, we don't want to hear any more. We've heard enough. I hope I am being understood a little bit better than you may have understood yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that it's always a positive finding for us when you say [unintelligible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course, I mean it's -- otherwise I wouldn't even dare of thinking of telling you, "please don't bring any evidence." Then the situation of Srebrenica during the period relevant to the indictment; namely, that it was cut off from the rest of BiH; that it was under constant siege; that it was sustaining or suffering from air and artillery bombardment. And when I say, I could add "constantly." And also, as regards, as the positioning of the Serb forces in and around Srebrenica. We don't need to hear more about that. And the opportunity that we have had to fly over Srebrenica and even drive around has strengthened our decision to tell you, please, don't bring any more evidence on this. We've heard enough.
