The refugees problem or problems in Srebrenica, and the critical condition under which the population of Srebrenica had to live during the period relevant to the indictment, and this relates not only to food shortage, which we dealt with for the purpose of Rule 98 bis, but also medical shortages and problems, hygiene issues, security concerns, and we are mentioning security concerns within the context of the macro-understanding of a military necessity. Sporadic electricity and telecommunications shortages. These we are satisfied already with the evidence that we've heard. You don't need to bring us more evidence to tell us that there were thousands of refugees, that they were sick, they were desperate, that -- we know it already. We don't want to hear or receive any evidence on the Srebrenica genocide of 1995. Next, and this is again a little bit different from where you were told -- what you were told yesterday. We don't need to hear more evidence to show that there was a military superiority of the Serbs, namely that the Serbs were better military-equipped than the Muslims and that, furthermore, they benefitted from the support of the JNA, or former JNA, and Serbia, and Serbia. We have enough evidence to put us in a position to tell you and your client you don't need to address this, you don't need to answer this. Next, the Muslim military capability in Srebrenica. This is the conclusion that we come to. The Muslim military capability in Srebrenica was largely dependent on weapons that could be captured from the Serb forces. This is what you were not told yesterday. You are being told today. We don't need to hear more evidence on this. We've heard enough. Then I come to the last point, which is very important and which you need to understand extremely well, not to have any misunderstandings. Reading through your first and second filing, we got, throughout, this -- the impression that you were very much concerned with the importance of proving to us the military necessity that there was to attack these various villages, all of them. We are telling you, you don't need to prove that. We are already granting you that, from all aspects, there was a military necessity and an urgent military necessity. It was a matter of life or death, to go on attack and try to secure food, medicine, weapons or whatever. This we have already told you for the purpose of 98 bis, within limited -- a limited context; we are amplifying now because now we are dealing with the entire Defence case. But we also want you to understand very, very clearly that the military necessity that we are interested in for the purposes of counts 3 and 5, 3 and 5, is the military necessity to destroy the houses that the Prosecution alleges to have been destroyed. It's not the military necessity to attack Fakovici or Ratkovici or Kravica or Jezestica. If you lose your time on that, you're free to do it. But you will be missing the wood for the -- the wood for the trees or vice versa, which we don't want you to miss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We are very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it clear. We certainly are not telling you, you don't need to adduce evidence or you are not going to be allowed to adduce evidence on the military necessity to burn down or destroy the houses, but we also want you to remember that you don't have the burden of proof, of proving that there was military necessity to do that. It's the Prosecution's burden to prove that there was no military necessity. We do not consider that at any time the onus of proof has shifted from the Prosecution on to the Defence. But you are intelligent enough, both of you and your client is not less intelligent than you are, to realise what kind of evidence the Prosecution has brought forward in this context. So ultimately what we are talking about for the purposes of counts 3 and 5 is: Was there indeed the destruction, the wanton destruction, that we have been told by some witnesses of the Prosecution that there was? You're free to address that. Who committed that destruction? Was it civilians? Was it soldiers, fighters? You're free to bring evidence on that, if you feel that you should address it, because you don't have a burden of proof. Were all houses destroyed without any military necessity at all or some of them were the result of collateral damages or some of them may have been destroyed by the Serbs themselves; if you want to bring evidence on that, you're free to bring evidence on that. Was Mr. Oric present during -- at one or more of these actions, you're free to bring evidence on that. Did his presence mean anything for the purpose of 7(1) responsibility or 7(3) responsibility, you're free to bring evidence on that. Was he in command there? Yes, you're free to bring evidence on that. But ultimately, did he have effective control on that? Yes, you're free to bring evidence on that. And then there is of course the question of having failed to punish, which I don't need to address myself. But in reality what I'm telling you is this: When we came to the conclusion that we will be suggesting that there will be so many witnesses and not more, and that you will have so much time and not more, it's because we feel that your case should be limited to what is necessary and not beyond, and we are telling you that as far as military necessity on the macro level, the need to attack Fakovici, you don't need to address it, and the other you don't need to address it. The need to defend Srebrenica at all costs, you don't need to address it. There is one area that was mentioned in your document that I will deal with very briefly. You seem to hint that you want to bring forward and build up the argument that the situation was so bad and became so worse that it seems that people were no longer responsible for their actions, that there was this kind of revenge feeling, and that the people in general behaved in such a manner that they were impossible to control. If that is a submission that you are making, then, okay, feel free to bring evidence, although you don't have a responsibility to -- of proving it. It may at the end of the day remain as a submission, and it's probably better addressed as a submission than by bringing forward someone to present it as a personal opinion. But that's up to you. As I said, the way you conduct your Defence is none of our concern, none of our concern. Then there is one final minor thing that will of course need to be addressed first between you and later on you will inform us. There is one witness that you want to bring forward, allegedly to confirm that he shot a video, a particular video, Pantus [phoen] or whatever. If that is the sole purpose of bringing him over, we don't need him. Especially if the Prosecution accepts the authenticity of that video. If the Prosecution has an objection to the authenticity of that video, yes, then please bring him over. Same applies to someone, some German fellow, who according to you took some photos. Again, if they are being contested as non-authentic by the Prosecution, then bring forward this -- that witness. If not, please don't bring him forward. We don't need him. I will not tell you whether we would need him or whether we would stop you if you brought Mr. Pantus to confirm that, yes, this is Srebrenica that you are seeing in this film. Yes, these are refugees eating in the streets in the cold of the night with fire. I don't know; if you need him to prove what we have already told you we don't need to be proved, bring him over. But it may cost you precious time that you might need for another witness. So at the end of the day this is the exercise that you will need to do. I think we have been more than clear, more than clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yeah, that is clear. We do have to obviously consider various matters and there are additional matters of how the calculation has been done of how many days and hours we sit, how much time we would have for filing a final brief. There are a number of other concerns totally independent from this but we will discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break now. I have to put a smiling face to the interpreters and technicians. I have abused of your patience but you realise as much as we do that we have a very important matter today on our agenda that we need to bring to a close. Please bear with us. I know that you are not going to be paid more or that it will not earn you any medals but, please, I thank you and please bear with us. Thank you. I think we can take -- we can have half an hour, half an hour. Do I expect any long interventions from your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Not an intervention as such but there will be a response. And we consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's continue where we left from. Mr. Jones, Madam Vidovic, would you like to take the floor now or would you also like to know the rest of what -- for the time being we propose to do and that we could change after having heard you? It's up -- it's just the same. More or less, you tell me what your preferences are. We could tell you how many witnesses we have in mind, we could tell you what length we consider adequate, and under what conditions. I mean -- but it's up to you. I mean, we can leave them until later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be useful for you to hear me first. I'll be brief. I don't wish to repeat anything that my colleague has already said, because what I have heard so far has made things much clearer to me now. First of all, before I move on to the matter in hand, I should just like to mention that yesterday at the end of the session, I told Mr. Von Hebel, and I don't think my colleague, Mr. Jones, was present at that point in time, that we are either going to be given the necessary time for our Defence case or we are not going to go ahead. That is the truth. That is what I told Mr. Von Hebel, and I'm just -- it's not something that Mr. Von Hebel thought up himself. I really did tell him that. I said that. And I said that because I was shocked by the fact that of the 72 witnesses proposed, we were given the proposal of bringing forward 19 witnesses. Of course, Your Honours - and you must understand me - I am very worried because I have a lot of responsibility on my shoulders to bring this case to a close, to see it through, together with my colleagues in the interests of our client, the Accused. I was very much concerned, especially concerned, about the matters that you said you did not wish to hear any more about, the facts you didn't wish to hear any more about. Because at that point we weren't quite clear of your position, what your position was, whether you thought that those matters, up until that point in time, had been clarified sufficiently or not. And, of course, now the situation is much clearer; so I'm not going to go back to those matters. However, linked to what you said here today, I should like to say several things, for example, with respect to ethnic cleansing. This is what can happen. I wish once again to reiterate and underline the fact that at no point was it our intention to present evidence and adduce evidence about everything that happened not only in eastern Bosnia but elsewhere as well, but when it comes to ethnic cleansing what will happen will be that this will overlap and coincide with several attacks are the subject of the indictment that is the first attacks. And so faced with a situation of that kind we are going to have to show you the context of the events themselves, or the event itself, especially as some of those ethnic -- instances of ethnic cleansing and the circumstances surrounding them will have direct consequences on what happened later when it came to the destruction of villages. So please understand us that we will only do this when it is absolutely necessary and relevant to establishing the fact of the military justification for burnings, not attacks but burnings, or if it is linked to any particular individuals, people, who were involved in these concrete attacks, and they were involved in specific ethnic cleansing or if it has something to do with the witnesses' credibility. And the same is true for the Serb attacks, because some of these individual attacks, or rather, the results of individual Serb attacks resulted in a counterattack in individual cases, a counterattack which is considered as an attack and is to be found in a count of the indictment. And I'm sure that you will recall that we presented certain documents on matters of that kind. Also, with the question of siege, we are going to mention some Serbian villages which were listed in the indictment and which are a part of the siege if this is relevant to ascertain and establish the events linked to the burning and arson. Now, what I am worried about at this point in time and why I asked to take the floor before we hear your decisions as to the number of witnesses, is this: For about eight months now we have listened to the Prosecution case and it was presented on the basis, among others, of paragraph 27 of the indictment. We simply cannot close our eyes to the fact that paragraph 27 of the indictment, which is to be found on page 7, states that the Muslim side, or, rather, Muslim forces, from the units in the municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica and Skelani, burnt and otherwise destroyed a minimum of 50 predominantly Serb villages and hamlets, and we have heard a series of witnesses here who did not only speak about the problems of these 13 villages listed in the indictment but they also spoke about Zaluzje, they spoke about Podravanje, they spoke about Azlica and Spat, and Obadi as well, and when we objected, and lodged our complaints, I'm sure the Court will remember, when we objected to the relevance of adducing evidence of this Court, the answer we were given was that it was relevant because the Prosecutor has the right to establish and prove like attacks. We cannot forget this part of the indictment and have to respond to it. So that is just one segment which prompted us to propose a certain number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. Are you putting on the onus of proving what the Prosecution may not have proved? Why do you say that you have to address this? Is your client being charged with this? He's only being charged under 3 and 5 of those -- three, four places with the adjacent hamlets. That's what we are interested about. I don't -- I'm telling you, we don't care about what happened in other places. It's none of our concern. It may come to serve only if it is necessary as a system of conduct. But do you have to address it? Why do you have to address it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you have precisely said is our concern, because we wish to prove the contrary, except if you are prepared to accept that thus far it was not systematic conduct that was afoot, and that it wasn't an example, the pattern -- as you know, the pattern of behaviour, the pattern of conduct, that's one aspects. The other aspect that I'm even more concerned about is this: It is the question that we cannot bypass. That in some of the attacks, in certain attacks, in the majority of attacks, especially in paragraphs 33 and 34, those there, a whole series of units are mentioned. First of all, the question of the subregion is mentioned and we have to deal with that absolutely because that implies the responsibility and accountability of our client, whether something like that existed and functioned or not, because it places him in command of the whole region, if it does, and within the frameworks of that, a whole series of units for which we claim that a number of them were not there at all, that they were not present where the Prosecutor says they were in the indictment, and concerned in the events. Whereas some other units which perhaps were present have absolutely nothing to do with our client or his subordinates. So that is what guided us to propose a larger number of witnesses, to put them forward. Now, I can agree that it would appear that certain witnesses are being multiplied and appear again and again. But if you look at this more closely, you will see that each witness speaks about his own unit. You saw the area yourselves. It is inaccessible, an inaccessible area, and it would be far easier for me if I would be able to cover all these attacks with just two witnesses, but it is just not possible. Especially for Bjelovac or Kravica or some other region, people who come from different enclaves to testify about one or two events and the possibility of my client to control them, his presence or the lack of his presence there. So please understand us. It would be far easier for us if you were to be able to do this with as few witnesses as possible. But it is not possible to do it with a small number of witnesses and you wouldn't have justice prevail if you did not allow us to show and demonstrate that our client was not in a position to control those units, as my first point, or that they were not under his control at all, or that the units were not subordinated to him in any way. I just cannot allow myself that luxury so please, would you consider the matter again? We are going to study the matter fully and we will do our best, wherever possible, to adhere to Rule 92 bis whereever possible. But also you must understand that we have been given very little time and in the space of two months we just will not be able to present our case. And just two more brief points, yesterday we raised the question, we said that we were not able to come by witnesses in the structure of witnesses that were listed, we noticed that we were not able to get two important categories of witnesses. The question of the authenticity of documents at this point in time and in this case is a crucial issue, and you told us in the beginning, when we were not prone to do this, and I don't think we should have accepted it, but we did accept it, that is to say that quite simply evidence is adduced without being confirmed by witnesses. We would like to show a certain number of documents or categories of documents to individual witnesses and for that we will require time. So we do have the 19 witnesses but we don't have the necessary time to adduce documents which we find indispensable to present the authenticity of defence. And the problem of Hamid Salihovic [phoen] and his documents is a very crucial problem, and any judgement without clarifying those issues will not be tenable. So it is in our interests, as it is in the entire -- in the interests of the entire trial, to clarify that particular matter. Also, the question of witness credibility. Now, why, in our cross-examination, we asked many questions about ethnic cleansing? Because with the first witnesses that came in, we noticed that they are giving a completely distorted picture of all this to the Trial Chamber so once again this boils down to the credibility of the witnesses. And apart from that, you will be able to see that we have very concrete and specific pieces of evidence having to do with the credibility of the Prosecution witnesses, and we even have reason to call witnesses back, and we of course know that expediency is an important matter for this trial and that is why we did not insist upon this; we thought we would be given enough time during the Defence case to adduce that evidence. So I now ask you to allot us as much time as possible for us to be able to challenge the credibility of certain witnesses, even if the Prosecutor does not agree with this. But I have many years of experience as a judge and I can say that I never saw as many witnesses lacking credibility as I have had here. And it is our task to challenge the credibility of the witnesses and so please give us a chance to do that. Give us enough time to challenge the credibility of the witnesses. Thank you, Your Honours. That is what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Basically, I think I have got very little to say about what you have mentioned, Madam Vidovic. You will get all the time that we think, in the circumstances, would be sufficient to address whatever you need to address. I repeat that the line of defence that you would wish to adopt, the areas that you wish to contest to the Prosecution, the emphasis on certain issues that you would like to make is your own decision, and it's none of our concern. We are not concerned with that. What we have done, very simply put, is the following. We have examined each witness, one by one. When I say examined, examined your statement of what the witness you propose would be testifying about. We have taken into consideration all those areas that we told you we don't need any further evidence on these. And therefore, at the end of the day, we have made our calculation, how much time would that have consumed? Also, how many witnesses less would we now need, because we won't need the other witnesses to deal with the various areas we told you, you need not address. And we had a long exercise that we did, together with our very capable staff, in identifying the various areas that you raise throughout the two documents, such as the impossibility or difficulties in securing communications with Tuzla, for example. We are not going to tell you, yes, that's important, that's not important. If you feel it is important, then it's included there and we have kept it there. Where we may be in disagreement is that you think, for example, that you can get one and two and three and four to testify about it, while looking at the summaries, we believe that it can easily be covered by one or by two. We are not going to tell you, bring one or two. We are going to tell you, deal with it in the way that you like, but you are going to have a limited number of witnesses that you bring over -- you can bring over or you may bring over, and a limited time. So if -- you have to be diligent, and you have to do a lot of homework, much more than the Prosecution did, because the Prosecution have a burden of proof and they can bring a mass of evidence and they have to bring a mass of evidence trying to prove their case. You don't have to prove anything. If the Prosecution suggested in the indictment, in paragraph 27 or whatever, that the Muslim forces went all out on 50 fronts doing this and doing that and you don't agree with it, at the end of the day, you're going to put a question to you but do I have to do anything about it? Because your client is not being charged with that. And my experience, and I'm sure everybody's experience in this Tribunal, is that, as we go along with the Defence case and the Defence witnesses, we witness a strengthening of the case of the Prosecution, and that is why, as we go along in other cases, with the case for the Defence, the number of witnesses that the Defence purports to bring forward in the beginning or plans, becomes lesser and lesser and lesser and there comes a day when they will tell you we are not going to bring any further evidence because the same thing would happen to your witnesses as happened with the insider witnesses and happens with the insider witnesses that the Prosecution brings forward sometimes, which remain insider witnesses but end up giving evidence much more in favour of the accused much more than in favour of the case for the Prosecution. So this is the risk. I am not going to get involved in your assessments. But I can assure you, Madam Vidovic, if you wants to deal with documents, authentication of documents, I don't know what you were told yesterday but we gave strict instructions to our senior Legal Officers that we are not clear exactly from the documents that you have filed, which documents we are talking about, because it's been put in a pretty vague manner. If we are talking of specific documents to be contested by specific witnesses then, of course, if you think that those documents are important for your case, bring them over. How long is it going to take to ask a witness, look at this document; do you consider it authentic or not authentic? Do you recognise the signature? What do you have to say? If you're considering a whole category of contesting a whole category of witnesses -- of documents, like all documents coming from this collection or from that collection or from that section, it's up to you. It's none of our business how you conduct your defence. But if you of course decide to bring over those witnesses, yes, we have made a calculation of how many of them there are, and if you're talking of a whole category of witnesses, I mean, if you bring one witness who is strong enough or two witnesses who are strong enough, do you need a third and a fourth and a fifth? But then, if you have six, seven, eight, nine, ten, separate documents, that you need to attack because you feel they are vital for your client's case and you need six, seven, eight witnesses, then bring those seven, eight witnesses and make sure that -- do not -- they do not consume of your time more than you need for perhaps more important... This becomes a question of management. Mr. Jones, myself, coming from the jurisdictions that we come from, we carry a lot of responsibility in doing this because if you make a mistake there, your client has had it. I mean, when I say "your client," it's not Mr. Oric; but this is something where you have to be extremely careful. Because you've given a number of witnesses, in my jurisdiction you're even told we don't want to hear this witness and we don't want to hear that witness because we do not consider his or her witness as relevant to any point in issue. We are not telling you that except with that young lady of next week, that -- I don't think we need to hear her. But if you want to bring her over, bring her over, but she will only testify on the things that we are allowing you to bring testimony -- to bring evidence upon. Not on a 15 year old telling us about distinguishing between this paramilitary group and that paramilitary group. Come on, let's -- I don't want to say much but you know, and Mr. Jones knows, what are the points in issue in this case. There aren't many. There are quite few, in fact. They are quite few. And some of them are more crucial than others. And there are areas where obviously the case of the Prosecution may be stronger than others. I'm not going to comment on that because that stands to be seen at the end of the day. But I suppose you are in a position to make an assessment just like we are. Now, today, we are not making our decision on the basis of whether we consider the case of the Prosecution strong here or stronger there or weak here or weaker there. That's, again, something, I say, pleasures yet to come. What we are concerned about is that we don't waste our time and our energy and our resources and that we stick to what is important. I told you, for example, authenticity of a video. I'm telling you, there, I am intervening and I'm telling you if it's just authenticity, don't bring him over, we don't need him but if it's authenticity of a department, it's up to you, make an assessment of whether a document is important for your case. Is it important to bring evidence to contest the authenticity of each and every document that you feel in your heart of hearts that is not a genuine, is not an authentic document, is it necessary? Because you don't have to prove the authenticity of these documents or the non-authenticity of these documents. It's the Prosecution that has to prove their authenticity. So again, it goes -- I am perhaps going beyond what I should be saying, but I don't think we are as yet on the same wavelength. There are -- I understand, I fully understand how you feel about certain things that happened in your country. I know, and I fully understand how you feel about certain things that you think are important for the case. If you continue thinking that way, it's up to you. It's your decision because I told you we are not going to get involved ourselves in what is necessary for your client for your client's defence. That's your problem, not ours, but we have made our calculations. Each -- we have a list of the various areas that you have mentioned in -- we have identified them and put them in pigeon holes and we have also the number of witnesses and who they are also, who would, according to your document, be testifying on this and on that. Many witnesses that could cover a series much things, a multitude of things. For example -- I mean, just to give you an example, a witness that would cover, for example, the War Presidency in Srebrenica, we are not taking any assumptions therefor granting you anything. It's up to you. I mean, you know -- is it important? Feel free to bring whatever evidence you want. But if you are clever you will find a witness who will deal with the question of the War Presidency, perhaps the question of the diary that we have had, perhaps the question of the military police, perhaps the role or alleged role of your client in all this, the relationship between the war president -- the military police, civil police, authority, and chain of -- if you can kill all those birds with one or two stones, that's up to you. You decide. It's a problem. It's a problem for you, it's a problem for us. What I can tell you is that we have made our assessment in -- without -- without being attached to the case as you are, because in our self -- we are detached from -- from your interests or from their interests. What I tried to make you understand, that you are dealing with three professional judges. At the end of the day, what you are going to get, and what the Prosecution are going to get, and believe me, we are experts at this, is a clinical, surgical intervention. We are going to pick up the various bits and pieces of the evidence and the law applicable and I can assure you that that is what is going to count, and it will be a neat, clear, surgical intervention. So if you want to go your way, go your way; go whichever way you like. There is the message that I'm trying to convey to you. I know that it is difficult. I know because I was a defence counsel myself for a long time, and I hated when the judges treated me like the way I am treating you. But I also realised that many a time they were right. And as we go along, you will realise that I am right. And at the end, you'll probably, both of you, realise that, that I am right, that there may be areas that you are so concerned about that we basically couldn't care for. So, please, put yourself in our position and prepare -- pretend to be the clinical surgeons that we are going to be, and stick to what is exactly and strictly relevant to the case, and what is relevant to the case, very much so, is yes, effective control, so then put it. So do you think we are going to tell you, on effective control you are limited only to one witness, two witnesses? Please, bring as many witnesses as you like on effective control. But you should also be able to know which effective control are we talking about? Is it Oric's effective control throughout the entire period on a regional level, on a municipal level? What are we talking about? We are talking of some inhuman and cruel treatment and deaths in two places over a very short period of time and an allegation that your client went there with evidence which goes in his evidence and evidence that goes against him. The whole question is -- no one is saying: He did it. No one is saying, Ah, you see, Oric, Oric, is personally responsible for the killing of these guys or for the -- what is being alleged is that ultimately he is responsible under 7(3). So that is what -- that is what you have to fight if you think there is a case to answer. The same as to the -- to the attacks, the wanton destruction attacks. The whole issue is not whether the Bosnian Muslims had a reason or not to attack. We are telling you they had every good reason to attack. They would have been very stupid and very irresponsible had they not attacked. But at the end of the day the question is the following: During these attacks, was it necessary to have these houses and all these houses destroyed? And there, there are various points that are important. Were they destroyed by troops, by civilians, or were they destroyed collaterally? Was there fighting -- they had to be destroyed because the Muslim forces were being attacked from there or whether they were -- I don't know. But if you feel these are relevant, then this is what you -- I mean, to attack that attempt by the Prosecution to prove that there was a systematic conduct on the part of the Muslim forces everywhere, yes, let's say that the Prosecution proved that. Are we going to conclude, therefore, that we don't need to go into the question of what happened in Jezestica or Kravica because, you know, they were on this rampage already from before? No. We would care very little on what happened before and concentrate on what happened which is relevant to our indictment. This is what I am telling you, this is going to be clinical. And if you don't understand that, we are very far from -- from understanding -- understanding each other, and this is what I'm trying to avoid by this entire exercise. Is there anything else, Mr. Jones, that would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And it's a matter of the calculations in arriving at how much time is required. I'll put some statistics forward so that we can all see what we are talking about. The Prosecution case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that when it suits you, yes, you make comparisons but when it doesn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is just for the purposes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not an equality of arms argument. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I understand that. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, no, it's simply to say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I lost the paper I had my notes upon. One moment, Mr. Jones. I don't know where I put it. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's a different point which is that we want a realistic assessment, actually, of what nine weeks or fen weeks means whether it comes to scheduling because the Prosecution case lasted - I'm subject to correction on any of this - but 15.491 minutes. If you divide that by 100 days, which excludes opening speeches and Rule 98 bis, you come to an average of 2 and a half hours per day of sitting. That's very important for really estimating how long the Defence case will need to be. Now, that's -- even if we sat five days a week, if the Trial Chamber sat five days a week, that would only yield 12 and a half hours a week on this average, 12 and a half hours of testimony. But very often in fact -- and during the Prosecution case we didn't sit five days a week and, in fact, the average works out at three days a week. That's 105 days of sitting divided by 35 weeks. So in fact even on the assumption of us having 20 witnesses, we would need twice as long as was predicted in the meeting yesterday. We wouldn't be able to finish by -- on the estimate of us having 3.25 hours or whatever per witness. In fact, that would take us to the beginning of December. It wouldn't take us to the end of October based on what we in fact -- the number of minutes and hours that we actually sit. Our calculation is that if the Chamber continues to sit as it's been doing, in other words an average two and a half hours per day on average three days a week, that gives seven and a half hours per week of testimony. In nine weeks, that means the Defence would have about 33.75 hours on the assumption we would have roughly 50 per cent after you add cross-examination by the Prosecution and questions by the judges, and that actually comes out to between an hour and an hour and a half for each witness. And so obviously that -- clearly, I'm not going to make comparisons there that, but Major Mujkanovic was six days, Priors Tucker, four days. I mean, we can't envisage a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You cannot, you cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We on average have an hour, an hour and a half for our witnesses it's completely unrealistic. So we would ask in any calculation of when the Defence case will end, that it be a realistic one based on actually hours and minutes of sitting and so, for example, if the Chamber is to say we grant you 200 hours or 100 hours or 500 hours, that's a lot more helpful than saying the case should be finished in nine weeks, i.e. by such and such a time. That's one point I want to make. I also do wonder and the Rule obviously -- the Rules provide for number of witnesses being set, but at the same time in light of what Your Honour has been saying about focusing clinically on the essentials, one suggestion comes to minds which is that, let's say, on Bijelovac there are 15 units allegedly involved, and we can bring in 15 witnesses but each of them only coming in for half an hour and saying I was in the Tokoljac [phoen] unit and we weren't anywhere near there, or I was in the Suceska unit and we were there, but we had nothing to do with Oric, or whatever, then it's certainly more useful to have more witnesses. It's more easy for us to be clinical than for us to have a fixed number of witnesses. So that thought springs to mind. I also want to mention two more points, very briefly, that we also felt there wasn't sufficient interval for filing for drafting post-trial briefs. Most cases, I think, again not to make comparisons, but six weeks to two months is normal. We were looking at two or three weeks for -- being envisaged for us to file post-trial briefs. And we just -- we consider that would not be enough -- I mean, it would be woefully inadequate for us. And fourthly, I wanted to mention that, of course, Rule 92 bis means that we could also cover a number of areas using that Rule, but again that's subject to the Prosecution not objecting to a large number of 92 bis statements being used, and finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or cross-examination being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but just indicate that depending of course on what Your Honours decides we may try to make extensive use of 92 bis. And finally for these witnesses coming up, the four we've scheduled we have had to do everything in a rush, and I think it would be impossible for us to bring in other witnesses at this stage. I mean, there's all the arrangements for visas and whatnot. No matter what happens they would have to remain the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you will have to make an effort there, Mr. Jones and I'm sure that if you make an effort, you will get there. Let me -- okay, anything else? Before I take the floor again, which will not be the last time, Mr. Wubben, I got the impression that you wanted to say something on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: First about the last issue regarding the last issue of the witnesses if there is any rescheduling of witnesses, new witnesses, well, my learned friend already addressed the issue of the organising and even if it is hard to do so and to overcome, there is also the issue then of the Prosecution who had to prepare for such new witnesses and need the time for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's rather hard to overcome if it is even possible. I want to address this. Also, of course, we will cooperate whenever possible and when it comes to the 90 bis strategy, if proposed by the Defence, we will look into the matter then during the trial. What I'd like to underline is I notice the kind of difference between the calculations from the 65 ter conference and today as proposed by Defence. I concede to the matter because I don't have a calculator with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not following you, the calculation in minutes and hours and -- okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dividing by 100. I can understand that it is two times 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a much more practical approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will leave that up to your judgement. Anyhow, what the discretion of this Bench is of today the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Shall I? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. It's a question on scheduling --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and courtroom availabilities. Never a dull moment, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Even on Friday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, on Friday, at least, you have the satisfaction of looking forward to the next couple of hours when it will be all over and you don't have to wake up tomorrow morning for another ordeal. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When it comes to the discretion of the Trial Chamber, indeed we have to address today the issue of the witness list and the discretion and decision by the Trial Chamber to clarify whether or not that list should be limited. Now, as I envisaged yesterday, I brought forward that it is appreciated when Trial Chamber is in advance transparent on such areas as defined as clarification to limit the witnesses and to suggest that to the Defence, as we see it in the Rules, to call upon the Defence to limit the case. It's much appreciated if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- we can't escape that. We have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That's why it's also appreciated by me when those areas are defined and I noticed that there were a kind of -- a number of 11 of such areas, most of them even falls within roughly speaking the areas that we would like to confirm and to stipulate or concede, and more or less during the trial we have often tried to get along with the Defence and tried to make an agreement and call upon to negotiate further with us. At the same time, Your Honour, when it is a clarification to call upon the Defence to limit their witness, it's of course another matter when those areas are defined as factual findings as such, and let me, please, further identify it for you because it might be a concern and it is a concern by me, but it might also be leading to an answer, a response, by this Trial Chamber that clarifies in such a way that I don't have the concern any longer. Now, when it comes to a factual finding as such, we are aware that we have findings in the 98 bis ruling and we have finding in the final decision-making, so that comes by the end of the year. And when these areas are labelled as factual findings, also a finding in favour of the Defence, we can only understand it in the framework of the clarification to call upon the Defence to limit their witness number as link it to the Defence case and not the overall case. So binding the Prosecution, even if they can cross the witnesses in the Defence case. Let me further underline, a factual finding being the same as such areas, one or more of those areas, might even be considered then, if not clarified further by the Trial Chamber, as being a designing, final finding by this Trial Chamber without being yet in a position to give a final judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I quite understand what you mean, but we tried to make that clear, that this is a commitment that we are making with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On these areas, you have our word, you don't need to bring evidence. That's it. We'll confirm our position as you say at the last moment, and we are not binding you. That's where Mr. Jones is completely -- completely right. This is not agreed facts. These are not agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have said and the responsibility that we have taken upon ourselves to tell the Defence you don't need to bring evidence on this, we are happy with what we have received already, or, like Srebrenica genocide 1995, because we do not attach to it any importance in relation to what Mr. Oric is standing -- has -- is standing charged with, we are not binding you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are not agreed facts. There is where Mr. Jones is right, but Mr. Jones and the Defence have got the commitment from the Trial Chamber that when we tell them you don't need to bring evidence on this, we are not going back on them and say, but, listen, this is -- this is all your fault because you didn't, after all, address these matters when you could have addressed them. So the bottom line is that -- I don't think we can make it clearer than this. We are not deciding the case. We are not even deciding officially these facts. But we are telling -- we are telling -- we are telling the Defence, "You -- you don't need to address these and you have our word that you will not suffer any consequences because you have not addressed these issues." This is basically it, which is done in all jurisdictions. I mean, we stop witnesses and we sometimes we tell them you don't need to testify on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This raises grave concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because ultimately these go, we don't want you to bring forward evidence because with we are satisfied with what we have and we are also satisfied that the evidence that there is, whether he agrees with it or whether he likes it or not is in your favour and not against.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just have a question in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- which is, what if -- if the Prosecution then cross-examines one of our witnesses to show that there was no military necessity for the attack on Bjelovac, then where do we stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we are not going to open doors as to whether there was any military necessity to attack Bjelovac. Please try to understand me. What is of concern to us is whether, in the attack on Bjelovac, it was persons for whom he may ultimately be responsible that wantonly destroyed houses there, and whether that was militarily necessary, not whether it was necessary to attack Bijelovac. We are not going to a-- it may be addressed now or later by the Prosecution but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But surely that means that the Prosecution shouldn't cross-examine on any of those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to allow to you to question witnesses on those points and therefore there should be no cross-examination. If they attempt, we will decide what to do. If what -- if our decision means that it reopens something for you that we told you it's closed, then we'll give you the opportunity. This is basically it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not -- we are not -- Judge Eser is making this clear. We need to make this clear. We are not telling you in any way you don't need to bring evidence when it comes to the aspect of military necessity to burn or destroy those houses. That is not included in what we said about the absence or the decision on our part not to require from you evidence on the military necessity to attack the various villages. That is one thing. The other military necessity is another. That is, I would say, your problem because I'm short of any other words for the time being. But that is what you need -- what or what I suppose you would need -- need to address if you feel that you should address it. But you don't need to address the question of whether there was any military necessity to attack Jezestica or Kravica or whatever. If the Prosecution brings -- adduces arguments which convinces us that we should open that chapter, then we are going to let you bring evidence on that. This is basically it. I think I made it clear. Mr. Wubben, we are sort of - how can I explain it in better terms? - we are telling the Defence there are some areas which have already been covered, partly because the witnesses of the Prosecution during examination-in-chief gave all the information that we think we need. Secondly, because upon cross-examination, some witnesses or others also gave all the information that we require, and together, we are -- we have reached now a stage where, if you try to bring further any more evidence on this or that particular subject, you will only be redundant in your evidence and in your submission. We don't need it any more. We are not telling that you with you don't need to adduce evidence in any area which we believe calls upon you to answer, sort of. Do you read me? I mean, we are talking of areas where we believe that you don't need, which we believe we don't need to address. Any other area which we may also think have enough -- received enough evidence, but which we think the evidence is such that it -- we would only benefit and increase our insight into the case if you adduce evidence, then it's up to you. We can't force you to bring evidence, obviously. You also have the right to remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's very clear to our point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to protest. My learned friend can interrupt you. I have the politeness not to interrupt you and it was my submission in which you asked me a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's not to be rude to my learned friend now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, proceed Mr. Wubben. Please, Mr. Jones, you will have your turn. Mr. Wubben, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I am obliged to accept that you will indeed have your turn but I would like to proceed. Because when it comes -- this becomes more and more clear to me but I guess the submission standing when finding is so looking like factual finding and the final factual finding. So it isn't. It's a clarification of -- that certain areas are covered and I would like to give the opportunity to Ms. Patricia Sellers to further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, let us make it clear, that we may end up ultimately confirming exactly these factual findings, so maybe we won't even need to go into some of them, and in all probability we won't even need to go into many of them, but at the end of the day, if you are unhappy with our decision, with our final decision, we have at no time tied your hand because this is not being presented as agreed facts. It's not even being presented as facts that the Trial Chamber is taking judicial notice of. So please do make the distinction. We are not taking judicial cognizance of these facts. We are just saying,"Mr. Jones, Madam Vidovic, we've heard enough on this. We don't want to hear any more." And we are not going to come back to you and tell you, "Ah, but listen these were the facts, you should have been wiser, you should have not listened to us, you should have brought evidence." So this is basically it. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just two points of clarification because I think it could be related to terminology. In terms of the attacks on the village, yesterday it was conveyed to us by a Senior Legal Officer that there was a macro-military necessity and a micro-military necessity. If I just might rephrase that I think you're referring to, you've heard sufficient evidence on the macro-military necessity but not necessarily, well, the Defence just in their submissions or evidence that, if they choose to bring it forward, in terms of the micro-military necessity as relates to wanton destruction. It does it not mean, if I understand correctly, that yes, the attack, for example of Bjelovac or Fakovici is legitimate in and of itself. I think you're saying that the attack occurred; that is not a relevant issue here. Our relevant issue is the military necessity as relates to the wanton destruction of the property and that relates back to the 98 bis. That's -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- basically what we are saying is this: That we don't want to hear any further evidence on whether it was militarily necessary to attack these places.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've heard more than enough but as to whether there was any military necessity to destroy these houses, we are not saying anything. We are just drawing the attention of the Defence that they don't have a burden of proof, they haven't got the burden of proof shifted on to them. The burden of proof of showing of proving that there was no military necessity to burn down these and destroy these houses, has always been and will always remain with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly understand that and accept that and proceeded basically in that manner. If I might just ask clarification on a subsequent issue, and that's when we are talking about the facts and having made a pact with the Defence, the Prosecution takes that to mean is that you've -- incognant [phoen] of facts that have come forward have come forward with the Prosecution case via Prosecution witnesses and via the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. These are not findings beyond a reasonable doubt which can only be made at the stage of the trial when the judgement is being considered. I believe this is what the Bench is saying to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's put it like -- I don't think that we have a question now because what needs to be proven beyond reasonable doubt at the end of the day is the guilt of the accused. So all the rest is relevant and relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think you understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is our same understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we are telling the Prosecution -- sorry, the Defence, that we are satisfied already with the fact that Srebrenica was under siege before, during, after, that this was an intensive siege, it involved the surrounding villages which were also part of the Srebrenica -- that they were being bombarded from the air and from the mountains, that the people were starving, that the hospital was a -- in a state of -- in a critical stage which is unbelievable, we could add what -- what we were told, but this was hell on earth. I'm telling the Prosecution, listen, we've heard enough, please -- the Defence, sorry. Not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, don't bring any further evidence on this. The way we are saying it also means that we are not then going on the Prosecution later on and say, listen, after all, this was not clear at all. There was -- there were problems. I mean we are not that sure that the situation in Srebrenica was that critical and frankly you should have addressed this matter. We are not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is a pact with the Defence. Yes, it is a pact with the Defence because if it's not a pact we cannot tell the Defence you don't need to bring evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. We understand that. That's the clarification we wanted, that we would not be limited neither in our cross-examination if any of those areas were touched on by the Defence or tangentially incurred or probably implied toward the credibility of one of the witnesses. But I think we were just trying to stay within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as relates to the factual findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: What I want you to be sure of is that you are dealing with a Trial Chamber that puts its top priority, number one, furthest. So if at any time during cross-examination you open up an area that we tried to close, then you will be opening up the opportunity for the Defence to bring forward more witnesses. Am I making that clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we will be quite alert to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we may stop you, just like we may stop witnesses of the Prosecution -- of the Defence if they try to go beyond what we consider to be relevant and necessary. And we can stop you, and -- provided we make sure that the entire process is fair and just. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We are still in the midst of our submission and Mr. Wubben conclude. One other issue that we felt that we might raise at this time because we are talking about scheduling, we are talking about facts as they relate to the case, and certainly, the Prosecution might, that depends on the evidence of the Defence, might have a rebuttal case, and so I realise that that has not been up unto this point considered within the scheduling. It rests a possibility, and I just want to alert Your Honour's attention to that since we are on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are fully aware of that. We are fully aware of that. But we prefer to leave that until later if we need it to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that finalised because that issue already covered my final part of this submission. I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So now, let's -- yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, now I think I do need to responds on a couple of items there because I'm concerned that the whole edifice upon which there was actually a means of reducing the Defence case, namely that findings, and I use the word "advisedly" because Your Honour said findings repeatedly, which would actually enable us to have something which we could rely upon and not bring evidence is going to crumble if it's diluted in the way the Prosecution is suggesting. If I may just briefly deal with that. For example, the example which my learned friend gave about -- that she understood you to be saying that military necessity in a macro sense was irrelevant, not that there was military necessity, well, I see what Your Honour said at page 46. You give the impression -- "you're very much concerned with the importance of proving to us the military necessity there was to attack these various villages, all of them, the ones in the indictment. We are telling you that you don't need to prove that. We are already granting you that from all aspects there was a military necessity and an urgent military necessity. It was a matter of life or death to go on attack and try to secure food, medicine, weapons, or whatever." Now, there, Your Honour is not saying it's irrelevant. You're saying we found there was military necessity and I want that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and we are not going back on that. But if the situation arises at any one given moment, Mr. Jones, that the Defence stand up -- the Prosecution stand up on cross-examination and they say, "Your Honours, this has become crucial are, we need to address it," and in our judgement we grant them time address it, then you are going to be granted equal opportunity, if not more, to address it when we had previously told you not to address it. So in other words you have our guarantee that if we are telling you, you don't need to address a matter now, today, today -- I mean not today, as we go along during the Defence case, we mean it. We are not playing any tricks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was my second point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words we are certainly not telling you this is the position today but it will change when we come until the final decision or to the final decision after that we have -- you have concluded your case. It's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's my second point, and it's a general one is-- my concern is this is a general one. My concern is if the Prosecution try to cross-examine on any of the findings which you made, so, for example, they seem -- they try to suggest to one of our witnesses that there weren't weapons in Fakovici, that the Serbs were not better equipped or any of the -- on any of those matters, then it's not just where we haven't examined in chief on that, then prima facie they should not be putting such questions. If they do, it's not just that we can re-examine on it, but actually we can go back and say, "Right, we want to reinstate five or ten witnesses who are going to deal with those points." I want to safeguard our position very clearly on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I think you are all perfectly capable of drawing a distinction. I made it clear that what is relevant for us is not whether there was any military necessity to attack Jezestica, Kravica, Bjelovac, and wherever. And we are saying it because we are satisfied on the basis of what we have heard that, to us, that is no longer in issue to the extent that requires you to address it. If that changes, we ourselves will tell you, Mr. Jones, there is a problem here. We told you that we were satisfied that there was -- that we -- that you didn't need to address the question of military necessity to attack Bjelovac. Now it seems that the evidence that is coming forward is such that we have to open that wide, wide open. And in that case, yes, we are going back on what we have told you, but you will be given the opportunity to bring forward all the evidence that you need. But then you ask me what if the Prosecution in cross-examining a witness in relation, for example, to the events in Fakovici, asks the question: Did you see any weapons in Fakovici? Of course that is a legitimate question. Come on, we are -- we are dealing, as far as I tried to convey to you, with the military necessity to destroy the houses or burn down the houses in Fakovici. So if the question the finding of weapons or the use of weapons in Fakovici during the attack becomes relevant, of course they put question. But there is something that we never told you, you don't need to bring evidence about. In other words, what happened in Fakovici, in Jezestica or in the other places, of course it's of concern to you. So the question -- the question -- the question that arises is whether there was military necessity to burn down those places. Anything that is relevant remains relevant for that particular purpose. But you don't have the burden to prove that there was military necessity. It's their responsibility to prove that there was no military necessity. So how -- that is going to fit -- I mean, what they are going to gain by asking questions whether there were any weapons or a cache of weapons in Jezestica or wherever, I mean, for the time being, it goes beyond me. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You might need to destroy places where weapons are kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But there is what I'm trying -- because we did -- we didn't go through this exercise blindfoldedly or in a path -- haphazard manner. We gave it a lot of thought. Yes, Mr. Wubben, sorry for having interrupted you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No I had finalised my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take your time. We are not in a hurry and what we don't succeed in finishing on today we will carry on to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, when I learned your response towards the concerns of my learned friend, again, when you address it in a way like you did, telling the Defence it is -- you shouldn't worry because we grant you this in such a way that you don't have to address it, and if the Prosecution addresses such a question, we have to decide upon -- to allow it, then the final outcome is that, yes, it is a clarification to limit the number of witnesses, and it will lead, perhaps, to that consequence, but also, that it has the same power as a factual finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, but if it has the same power as factual finding then it is a factual finding as such, and then -- then I would like to suggest, and advise the Trial Chamber, to be very clear whether or not it is a factual finding and whether or not the Prosecution is allowed to also include in there -- in the Defence case, relevant questions regarding that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if the moment you include or you try, first of all, you will only be able to include them if we allow you to. That's number one. And you will have to justify why you want to then reopen those areas that we have closed. And secondly, if we allow you to reopen those areas, then they are going to be allowed to reopen those areas. So this is why I'm telling you these are not factual findings in the way that you are having it in your mind. These are factual findings, yes, to an extent, that we are telling them, telling the Defence rebus sic stantibus, things as they are, you don't need to address these matters for the time being. If the situation changes, yes, we will call upon them to address these matters. This is -- this is it. But as the situation is at present, they don't need to address it, in our judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay. So no factual finding as such with a view to the final judgement or the 98 bis and second, I request then Trial Chamber in their written ruling on Monday to be, if possible, to be clear in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, we will only say these are the areas that the Defence need not address in the present circumstances. If the circumstances change, we are going to call on them -- listen, situation has changed and now you are free -- so now, let me move to the other areas that we have -- first of all, I wish to thank you both, Prosecution and Defence, for your very -- for the very constructive way in which you have cooperated with the Trial Chamber in trying to iron out the differences that resulted after yesterday's 65 ter meeting. It doesn't mean to say that we are reaching an agreement. Far from it. It doesn't mean to say that whatever we decide will go down well with either or both of you but it will be our decision anyway. We revised again, reviewed again, dedicating a lot of hours, which, considering our age, is quite a feat, to your documents again, going through each witness, one by one, taking off those elements that we don't need to hear about, other elements that we think are not necessary, overlapping, repeated, repetitions, and whatever. I told you also that we -- the indication that you had yesterday, two witnesses here, three witnesses there, two witnesses here, three witnesses there, was more or less a reflection of the exercise that we had been doing. There were various aspects that you don't -- it doesn't appear to us that were dealt with yesterday, not because of any fault of Mr. Von Hebel, but because of the electrically charged atmosphere that developed as you went along, which resulted in what I consider may be a premature conclusion to the meeting. We have come to the following conclusion, having again gone through the entire list, going through -- through the very sterling work that our staff did, working long hours with us as well. We have come to the conclusion that the case for the Prosecution can be finished by the end of September. Am I just speaking of weeks? I know that basically sometimes it happens that one particular week we cannot sit because there is courtroom maintenance or one other particular week we cannot sit because of this or because of that. We are drawing a distinction between days when we cannot sit because of reasons beyond our control and days when we do not sit because of reasons that are attributable only to shortcomings on the part of the Defence. We are also aware that if during a particular sitting an hour or two are lost on the submissions on a particular issue, that's one hour or two taken from the time of the Defence. So the position is as follows: We are saying case for the Prosecution ends end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Case for Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Case for the Defence -- case for the Defence ends end of September but if we have lost three days, four days, five days, through no fault of the Defence and simply because we just couldn't -- we couldn't sit, then obviously those are going to be recovered and given back to the Defence. Similarly, if there are hours lost because of pleadings and other incidents that may arise, those will be accumulated and given back to the Defence. Any time lost because of shortcomings, for example the Defence has failed to bring any witnesses, we will take into consideration any submission that there may be. If we think that there is a justification, that time lost will be recovered. If there is no justification, in our opinion, that will be time lost. After the end of September, there will also be three additional days, during which the Defence will be allowed to bring forward evidence, witnesses, of a mitigatory nature. You know that in our system, we do not finish first the stage of the trial stage arriving at a conviction and then proceed with a separate hearing on sentencing. We don't have that system here. So essentially, the Defence, unfortunately, finds itself in the situation where it has its hands tied. Any evidence in mitigation, including, for example, strangely enough, evidence on remorse, must necessarily be brought forward during the case of the Defence stage. This is how it is. And we are not going to change it. So there will be three further days during which the Defence will be allowed to adduce such evidence, if they want to, because, Mr. Jones, we are making it clear that we are not forcing you in any way to adduce evidence of mitigation. That's something that you need to think about, and Madam Vidovic, and decide upon. We notice, for example, that in your list of witnesses, there are several witnesses that you purport or propose to bring forward to testify on the character of the Accused. At this point in time, the character of the Accused can be important from a substantive point of view or it can be important from just a mitigation -- mitigatory factor. So you will need to do this exercise in your mind, see whether you would prefer to bring these witnesses together in those three days -- in those three days, but the number of witnesses that we are going to grant you is not going to increase or decrease depending on how many witnesses you would like to bring in mitigation. We are going to give you a number of witnesses, some of which you can of course bring in mitigation during those three days which would leave you untouched. The remaining or the preceding period of -- until the end of September, which you can utilise for the remaining witnesses. The number of witnesses that we have come to, having taken into consideration, again, the list, your representations made to our Senior Legal Officer yesterday, and upon revising again the list, we have come to the conclusion that you can address in a more than satisfactory manner, ensuring a fair trial and a good defence for your client, with the number of 30 witnesses. If at any time the situation changes, I cannot for the time being anticipate how and when or why, but if at any time the situation changes, to an extent that we are satisfied that we would need either more time or more witnesses on any particular issue, we will decide on that as we go along. But for the time being, our decision will be that you will have 30 witnesses, those will include also witnesses on character and any other mitigatory factors that you need to conclude by the 30th of June -- of September, plus those extra three days plus any days, any time, that we will need to recover to complete the time that we need -- we think that you need to complete your exercise. This will be of course reduced into writing. We hope to be able to have it ready Monday. I am hopeful but of course we also depends on our staff that have been working overtime time throughout the entire week and you need to realise that we also have an interest in making sure that they are not overworked and not overstressed because then the whole team will suffer, but Monday, we hope to be able to hand down this decision. Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this has dramatic implications for us. I would seek certification of leave to appeal on the basis of the oral decision. We have to move very quickly to safeguard the position of our client, which as I said at the outset we think is -- fundamentally compromises a fair trial for our client and we -- I think, I don't know if Your Honour wishes me to address you at length on Rule 73 and the criteria, but I think it's obvious that this -- the decision will have an impact on the fairness of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have every right to appeal and we will consider granting you certification or not but please do file, have it ready, because Monday you will get the decision. And if you file it afterwards, I mean, after we hand down the decision, we promise you we will come down with our decision the following day, at the maximum, and if there is an appeal, exert all the influence of -- that we can, if we grant certification, we'll -- we'll communicate to the Appeals Chamber the need to have this decided with the utmost urgency. However, I also want to make clear that no appeal will stop us from proceeding any further. In other words, be prepared on Monday, this is not going to take from our trial time. Because it was a -- it will be a written decision filed formally. So Monday, be prepared with Edina or whoever you wish to bring forward as your first witness. That is none -- none of our concern. And we will move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour made that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, and this is in your interest because if you take the other approach that you hinted at this morning, say, we will not bring any evidence until this is decided by the Appeals Chamber, we will move ahead just the same and if the Appeals Chamber ultimately agrees with our decision, then we are not going to say, yes, but now -- so, we now start the nine weeks counting from today. We are not going to do that. So I think I am being -- I'm sorry, I have to deal with you this way but this is the way which any other judge would have to deal with you, given the circumstances. It has got nothing to do with -- I can -- with Judge Brydensholt or Judge Eser staying here. I can assure you that if I go today to Judge -- to President Meron and tell him we have a problem, we won't finish by end of November, we need -- end of December, he is not going to question it one single moment. But I will not go to President Meron and ask him for an extension to January or to December if I am sure in my heart of hearts having examined that we can easily finish by a certain date. We may be wrong. It may misfire. And if it misfires, I mean I carry the responsibility together with my colleagues and we will go to President Meron and we will say we need more days. But if we don't need more days I am not going to President Meron.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I ask that we sit in the afternoon on Monday. I think we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sitting in the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- just to give us time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Monday morning, we were sitting in the morning up until about when we were still in Bosnia. That changed when we were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I know there were moves afoot to maybe have a morning sitting and since we will need the morning for the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I tried. Yeah, no, no, no, it's -- we won't be sitting in the morning, but we will be sitting in the afternoon. That's number one. Secondly on Thursday - I think I told you this already, no? - that on Thursday we have to switch to the afternoon, and from Courtroom III to Courtroom I because this courtroom is needed by Judge Liu in the Halilovic case, and he can only hold the sitting in this courtroom. I mean, because of technical reasons. So I took the liberty of saying, yes it's not going to -- it would have been different had it been from moving it from the afternoon to the morning because it may have affected your ability to -- that's the -- that's the -- that's the position. There are a few other things that we need to address. There is a filing by the Prosecution relating to the third amended indictment. There are two filings. One original, one additional. Do you have any comments on your part, Mr. Vidovic -- Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
